30268.q: Which “trench” divided Switzerland during the First World War?
30268.e: Many German-speaking Swiss sided with Germany, many French-speaking Swiss with France. This divide was called the “trench”.
30268.m: In the First World War a trench divided German-speaking and French-speaking Switzerland.

30269.q: Why did many soldiers' families fall into hardship during border guard duty from 1914 to 1918?
a: There was no compensation for lost wages
30269.e: Anyone doing military service got no pay from their employer and no compensation for lost wages. Many families became poor because the breadwinner was away for months.
30269.m: Without compensation for lost wages, many soldiers' families suffered hardship in the First World War.

30271.q: What did Switzerland, as a neutral country, have to avoid in the First World War?
a: Favouring one side in the war
30271.e: Being neutral means keeping out of the war and not supporting either side. In 1917 a Federal Councillor had to resign because he had broken this rule.
30271.m: Neutral means not favouring one side in a war.

30272.q: Which big strike followed the hardship of the war years in November 1918?
30272.e: Many working families suffered hunger and hardship during the war. In November 1918 about 250,000 people went on strike all over Switzerland.
30272.m: The National Strike took place in November 1918.

30273.q: About which woman from the Jura did the soldiers on border duty sing a well-known song?
30273.e: Gilberte Montavon served the soldiers in the inn at Courgenay. The song about her became very popular, and a film about her came out in 1941.
30273.m: Gilberte de Courgenay became famous through a soldiers' song.

30274.q: In which year did the Swiss National Strike take place?
30274.e: The National Strike lasted from 12 to 14 November 1918. It is the biggest strike in Swiss history.
30274.m: The National Strike took place in November 1918.

30276.q: What did the strikers do during the National Strike of 1918?
30276.e: In a strike, people stop working to push through their demands. In 1918 the machines stood still in many factories.
30276.m: During the National Strike people stopped working.

30277.q: Roughly how many people took part in the National Strike of 1918?
30277.e: About 250,000 workers downed tools. Railway workers went on strike too, so in many places no trains ran.
30277.m: About a quarter of a million people took part in the National Strike.

30278.q: Which demand of the National Strike was only met in 1971?
30278.e: Women's right to vote was one of the nine demands of 1918. But Switzerland only introduced it at federal level in 1971.
30278.m: Women only got the vote in Switzerland in 1971.

30279.q: Which demand of the National Strike had largely been put into practice by 1919 and 1920?
30279.e: Shortly after the strike, working hours in factories were limited to 48 hours a week.
30279.m: The 48-hour week was a quick success after the National Strike.

30280.q: Whom did the Federal Council send against the strikers in the National Strike of 1918?
30280.e: The Federal Council had troops march in. After three days the strike committee called off the strike.
30280.m: The Federal Council used the army against the National Strike.

30281.q: Which social insurance went back to a demand of the National Strike but was only introduced in 1948?
30281.e: In 1918 the strikers demanded old-age and disability insurance. The people said yes in principle in 1925, but AHV only came in 1948.

30282.q: In which year was the National Council first elected by proportional representation?
30282.e: On 26 October 1919 the first National Council election under proportional representation took place. Before that the majority system applied.
30282.m: Since 1919 the National Council has been elected by proportional representation.

a: Seats according to the parties' share of the votes
Whoever has the most votes gets all the seats
The seats are drawn by lot
30283.e: Under proportional representation, parties get as many seats as their share of the votes. That way smaller parties get into parliament too.
30283.m: In proportional representation, seats follow the share of the votes.

30284.q: What is the voting system called that applied to the National Council before 1919?
30284.e: In majority voting, whoever has the majority of the votes wins. For decades this mainly benefited the Radical party.
30284.m: Before 1919 the National Council was elected by majority voting.

30285.q: Which party lost its absolute majority in the National Council in 1919 because of proportional representation?
30285.e: The Radicals had dominated the National Council since 1848. In 1919 they lost over 40 seats and with them their absolute majority.
30285.m: With proportional representation, the Radicals' dominance in the National Council ended in 1919.

30286.q: Which party almost doubled its seats in the National Council in 1919?
30286.e: The Social Democratic Party benefited greatly from the new voting system. Its number of seats in the National Council almost doubled.
30286.m: In 1919 the SP won many seats thanks to proportional representation.

30287.q: How was proportional representation for the National Council introduced?
a: Through a decision of the Federal Council
Through a ruling of the Federal Supreme Court
Through an order from the general
30287.e: On 13 October 1918 the people accepted a popular initiative for proportional representation. Earlier attempts had failed.
30287.m: Proportional representation for the National Council goes back to a popular initiative.

30288.q: Which present-day party grew out of the farmers' and citizens' parties?
30288.e: In 1919 the farmers' and citizens' parties won many seats in the National Council for the first time. The Swiss People's Party later grew out of them.
30288.m: The SVP goes back to the farmers' parties.

30289.q: Who was allowed to vote in the first proportional election of the National Council in 1919?
30289.e: Women only got the right to vote and stand for election at federal level in 1971. In 1919 only Swiss men voted.
30289.m: In 1919 only men could vote for the National Council.

30290.q: In which Swiss city did the League of Nations have its headquarters?
30290.e: The League of Nations started work in 1920 and chose Geneva as its seat. That is why Geneva is still a city of international organisations today.
30290.m: The League of Nations had its headquarters in Geneva.

30291.q: Which US president proposed founding the League of Nations?
30291.e: In his Fourteen Points of 1918, Woodrow Wilson called for a league of nations. It was meant to keep the peace after the First World War.
30291.m: Woodrow Wilson was the father of the idea of the League of Nations.

30292.q: How did Switzerland join the League of Nations in 1920?
30292.e: On 16 May 1920 the people and the cantons approved joining. The majority of the cantons was very narrow.
30292.m: The Swiss people voted to join the League of Nations in 1920.

30293.q: Which large building was built for the League of Nations in Geneva?
30293.e: The League of Nations moved into the new Palais des Nations in 1936. Today the UN uses the building.
30293.m: The Palais des Nations in Geneva was built for the League of Nations.

30294.q: What did Switzerland want to remain even as a member of the League of Nations?
30294.e: Switzerland joined the League of Nations in 1920 but wanted to stay neutral. So it did not have to take part in military punishments.
30294.m: Switzerland stayed neutral in the League of Nations too.

30295.q: What was the main aim of the League of Nations?
a: To keep peace in the world
30295.e: After the First World War, countries wanted to prevent new wars. For this they founded the League of Nations in 1920.
30295.m: The League of Nations was meant to keep the peace.

30296.q: In which year was the League of Nations dissolved?
30296.e: The League of Nations had not been able to prevent the Second World War. In 1946 it came to an end, and the UN took over its tasks.
30296.m: The League of Nations was dissolved in 1946.

30297.q: What was the Spiritual National Defence of the 1930s mainly directed against?
30297.e: Switzerland wanted to strengthen its own culture and democracy against the ideas coming from Germany and Italy. Later the movement also turned against communism.
30297.m: The Spiritual National Defence strengthened Switzerland against Nazism and fascism.

30298.q: Which big exhibition in Zurich in 1939 is part of the Spiritual National Defence?
30298.e: The National Exhibition of 1939, known as the Landi, showed the variety and strength of Switzerland. Just before the war it brought people closer together.
30298.m: The Landi of 1939 strengthened Swiss unity.

30299.q: Which language became the fourth national language through a popular vote in 1938?
30299.e: In February 1938 the people voted by a large majority for Romansh as a national language. It also sent a signal to Italy, which called the language an Italian dialect.
30299.m: Romansh has been the fourth national language since 1938.

30300.q: Which cultural foundation was created in 1939 as part of the Spiritual National Defence?
30300.e: The Culture Message of 1938 proposed an office to promote Swiss culture. That is how Pro Helvetia came about, and it still supports art and culture today.
30300.m: Pro Helvetia was founded to promote Swiss culture.

30301.q: How were the ideas of the Spiritual National Defence mainly spread?
30301.e: Films, books, songs and the Landi of 1939 showed what makes Switzerland special. This was meant to bring people closer together.
30301.m: The Spiritual National Defence used films, books and exhibitions.

30302.q: What aim did the Spiritual National Defence have within Switzerland?
a: To strengthen unity between all parts of the country
To introduce a single national language
30302.e: The movement stressed the variety of languages and cultures as a strength. Shared values were meant to overcome divisions between classes and parties.
30302.m: The Spiritual National Defence aimed to unite Switzerland despite its variety.

30303.q: Which Swiss legendary hero was shown especially often during the Spiritual National Defence?
30303.e: William Tell stood for freedom and resistance against foreign rulers. That is why his story was often told in films and plays.
30303.m: William Tell stood for Switzerland's will to be free.

30304.q: What material is the famous Landi chair of 1939 made of?
30304.e: Hans Coray designed the light aluminium chair with holes for the National Exhibition. Today it counts as a classic of Swiss design.
30304.m: The Landi chair is a design classic made of aluminium.

30305.q: Which event interrupted the Landi for a few days in September 1939?
30305.e: On 1 September 1939 the Second World War began, and the army was mobilised. The exhibition closed for three days and then reopened.
30305.m: Mobilisation in 1939 briefly interrupted the National Exhibition.

30306.q: What hung along a long exhibition path at the Landi in 1939?
30306.e: The flags of many Swiss municipalities hung along the Höhenstrasse. It showed the history and character of Switzerland.
30306.m: Flags of the municipalities hung at the Landi.

30307.q: What does the statue “Readiness to Defend” from the Landi of 1939 show?
a: A man putting on his uniform jacket
30307.e: The figure by Hans Brandenberger stands for the will to defend the country. A marble copy stands in Zurich today.
30307.m: The statue “Readiness to Defend” showed Switzerland's will to defend itself.

30308.q: What could you ride high above Lake Zurich at the Landi in 1939?
30308.e: A cable car linked the two lakeshores of the Landi. It drew huge crowds.
30308.m: At the Landi a cable car ran over Lake Zurich.

30309.q: What did the “Landi village” at the 1939 National Exhibition show?
30309.e: The Landi village had houses in the style of different regions. It showed country life in Switzerland.
30309.m: The Landi village showed rural Switzerland.

30310.q: What did people later mean by the “Landi spirit”?
30310.e: Just before the war, the Landi strengthened the Swiss people's sense of community. This feeling was called the Landi spirit.
30310.m: The Landi spirit stood for Swiss togetherness before the war.

30311.q: What hung on the wall in many Swiss inns and living rooms during the Second World War?
a: A picture of the Emperor of Austria
30311.e: Guisan was extremely popular during the war. His portrait hung in many pubs, shops and homes, and some can still be seen there today.
30311.m: General Guisan's portrait hung in many Swiss living rooms.

30312.q: Who elected Henri Guisan as general in 1939?
a: The people at the ballot box
30312.e: The general is elected by the United Federal Assembly, meaning the National Council and the Council of States together. Guisan got 204 of 229 valid votes.
30312.m: The general is elected by the Federal Assembly.

30313.q: Henri Guisan, born in 1874, became general in late summer 1939. How old did that make him?
30313.e: Guisan came into the world in October 1874. So at his election at the end of August 1939 he had reached the age of 64.
30313.m: Henri Guisan became general at the age of 64.

30314.q: In which canton did Henri Guisan live?
30314.e: From 1902 Guisan farmed the Verte Rive estate in Pully near Lausanne. He died there in April 1960.
30314.m: Henri Guisan lived in the canton of Vaud.

30315.q: Whom did General Guisan meet secretly in 1943, which later caused much controversy?
a: A senior officer from Nazi Germany
30315.e: Guisan met the SS officer Walter Schellenberg. Many saw this as dangerously close to Germany.
30315.m: Guisan's secret meeting with an SS officer in 1943 remained controversial.

30316.q: What did General Guisan do in 1945 to mark the end of active service?
a: He held a final briefing with his officers
He was elected to the Federal Council
30316.e: Guisan gathered about 400 officers at Jegenstorf Castle near Bern. After that he stepped down as general.
30316.m: Guisan ended active service in 1945 with a final briefing.

30317.q: What was General Henri Guisan's mother tongue?
30317.e: Guisan came from French-speaking Switzerland and commanded the 1st Army Corps there before his election. He was the first French-speaking general since Dufour.
30317.m: Henri Guisan came from French-speaking Switzerland.

30318.q: In which year did the Rütli Report take place?
30318.e: The Rütli Report took place on 25 July 1940. Shortly before, France had surrendered to Germany.
30318.m: The Rütli Report took place in summer 1940.

30319.q: Who came to the Rütli meadow for the Rütli Report in 1940?
a: The senior officers of the army
The Federal Councillors and their families
School classes from all over Switzerland
30319.e: General Guisan called the senior army officers to the Rütli. So almost the entire army leadership gathered in one place.
30319.m: At the Rütli Report Guisan spoke to the senior officers.

30320.q: Which new defence strategy did Guisan explain at the Rütli Report?
30320.e: Guisan explained that the army would pull back into the Alps and defend itself there. This was meant to show that Switzerland would resist.
30320.m: At the Rütli Report Guisan presented the Réduit.

30321.q: What situation made the Rütli Report in summer 1940 especially important?
a: Switzerland was surrounded by the Axis powers
Switzerland had just won a war
30321.e: After France's defeat, Germany and Italy surrounded Switzerland almost completely. Many doubted the will to resist, and Guisan wanted to strengthen it.
30321.m: In 1940 the Rütli Report aimed to strengthen the army's will to resist.

30322.q: What danger did the Rütli Report pose for the army?
a: Almost the entire army leadership was in one place
The soldiers had to walk a long way
30322.e: An attack could have left the army almost without leaders in one blow. Even so, Guisan stuck to this symbolic meeting.
30322.m: The whole senior army leadership gathered at the Rütli Report.

30323.q: What is the easiest way to get to the Rütli meadow?
30323.e: The Rütli lies on Lake Uri and can only be reached on foot or by boat. The officers also travelled across the lake in 1940.
30323.m: The best way to get to the Rütli is by boat.

30324.q: Why did General Guisan choose the Rütli of all places for his briefing in 1940?
a: Because it is a symbol of the founding of the Confederation
Because the biggest barracks stood there
Because it is right next to the Federal Palace
Because it is the highest mountain in Switzerland
30324.e: The Rütli counts as the place of the Federal Oath of 1291. Guisan chose it to show courage and the will to resist.
30324.m: For Guisan the Rütli stood for freedom and unity.

30325.q: What does the French word “Réduit” mean in Swiss military history?
a: Plan of attack to the north
30325.e: A réduit is a fortified place to retreat to. In an emergency the army would pull back into the Alpine region and defend itself there.
30325.m: The Réduit was the Swiss army's Alpine fortress.

30326.q: Which mountain massif formed the centre of the Réduit?
30326.e: The Gotthard massif lay at the centre of the Alpine fortress. Together with Sargans and Saint-Maurice it formed the most important fortress areas.
30326.m: The Gotthard was the heart of the Réduit.

30327.q: Which fortress in the Valais was one of the three great cornerstones of the Réduit?
30327.e: Saint-Maurice blocked the way into the Rhone Valley. Together with the Gotthard and Sargans it formed the three most important fortresses.
30327.m: Saint-Maurice was one of the three great Réduit fortresses.

30328.q: Which fortress in eastern Switzerland belonged to the Réduit?
30328.e: Sargans Fortress blocked the way from the Rhine Valley into the Alps. It formed the eastern cornerstone of the Réduit.
30328.m: Sargans was the eastern cornerstone of the Réduit.

30329.q: What did Switzerland threaten an attacker with as part of the Réduit strategy?
30329.e: In an emergency, tunnels and bridges at the Gotthard and Simplon would be blown up. That would have made the important links between Germany and Italy useless.
30329.m: The Réduit threatened to blow up the Alpine transit routes.

30330.q: What was a controversial drawback of the Réduit strategy?
a: The Central Plateau was hardly defended
The army had to go abroad
30330.e: Most people lived and most factories stood on the Central Plateau. In an attack, the population there would have been left largely unprotected.
30330.m: The Réduit largely left the densely populated Central Plateau to the enemy.

30331.q: After which military event of 1940 was the Réduit decided on?
a: After the USA entered the war
30331.e: In June 1940 France surrendered, and the Axis powers surrounded Switzerland almost completely. Defending the long border no longer seemed possible.
30331.m: After the fall of France in 1940 Switzerland relied on the Réduit.

30332.q: Roughly how much did Switzerland's farmland grow during the Cultivation Battle?
30332.e: Farmland grew from about 183,000 to about 352,000 hectares. That is almost twice as much.
30332.m: In the Cultivation Battle farmland almost doubled.

30333.q: Apart from food, what did the Cultivation Battle mean for people?
a: A symbol of the will to hold out
30333.e: Almost everyone joined in, including children and city dwellers. So the Cultivation Battle strengthened the feeling of getting through the crisis together.
30333.m: The Cultivation Battle strengthened unity in wartime.

30334.q: Which foods were never rationed in Switzerland during the Second World War?
30334.e: Thanks to the Cultivation Battle there were enough potatoes, vegetables and fruit. So these foods never had to be rationed.
30334.m: Thanks to the Cultivation Battle, potatoes, vegetables and fruit stayed freely available.

30336.q: How did the vegetable harvest change during the Cultivation Battle?
30336.e: Far more vegetables were planted in fields, gardens and parks. The harvest rose to about four times as much.
30336.m: The vegetable harvest quadrupled in the Cultivation Battle.

30337.q: During which event did the Cultivation Battle take place?
30337.e: Friedrich Traugott Wahlen presented his plan in November 1940. The Cultivation Battle lasted until the end of the war in 1945.
30337.m: The Cultivation Battle took place in the Second World War.

30338.q: Where else were vegetables and potatoes planted during the Cultivation Battle?
a: Even in city parks and on sports fields
30338.e: Almost every free piece of land got used, even parks and sports fields in the cities. About 500,000 small growers helped.
30338.m: In the Cultivation Battle vegetables were even planted in parks.

30339.q: In which year did regular food rationing begin in Switzerland during the Second World War?
30339.e: On 30 October 1939 sugar, pulses, cereal products, fats and oils were rationed. Other foods were added later.

30340.q: What was required twice a week in Switzerland from May 1941?
30340.e: On two days a week, butchers and restaurants were not allowed to offer meat. This was meant to save meat.
30340.m: During the war there were two meatless days a week.

a: Buying lots to store out of fear
30341.e: When people fear shortages, they buy large amounts. That is why in 1939 the federal government briefly banned buying important foods.
30341.m: Panic buying means buying to store out of fear.

30342.q: From when was meat also rationed in Switzerland during the Second World War?
30342.e: From March 1942 meat was only available with coupons. Before that, people had tried to save meat with meatless days.
30342.m: Meat rationing in Switzerland began in 1942.

30343.q: Why was food rationed during the Second World War?
a: So that there was enough for everyone
So that people would lose weight
So that shops would earn more
So that people had to cook less
30343.e: Many goods could no longer be imported. With rationing, every person got a fair amount.
30343.m: Rationing shared out scarce food fairly.

30344.q: Why were the ration coupons printed on special paper?
a: So that they could not be forged
So that they could be eaten
So that they glowed in the dark
30344.e: The coupons were printed on special paper made under strict control. This was meant to prevent forgeries.
30344.m: Special paper protected the ration coupons from forgery.

30345.q: What did the “J stamp” in German passports mean from 1938?
a: The holder was a young person
30345.e: Germany stamped a red “J” in the passports of Jewish people. This let Swiss border officials recognise them at once and turn them away.
30345.m: The J stamp marked the passports of Jewish people.

30346.q: Between which two states was the J stamp agreed in 1938?
30346.e: On 29 September 1938 Switzerland and Germany agreed on the marking. Switzerland wanted to be able to recognise Jewish refugees at the border.
30346.m: The J stamp goes back to an agreement between Switzerland and Germany.

30347.q: What was the phrase “The boat is full” from 1942 meant to say?
a: Switzerland would take in no more refugees
30347.e: Federal Councillor Eduard von Steiger compared Switzerland to a full lifeboat. He used this to justify turning many refugees away.
30347.m: “The boat is full” justified turning refugees away.

30348.q: What did Switzerland decide about Jewish refugees in August 1942?
a: It closed the border to them
It took them all in at once
It paid for their onward journey
30348.e: On 13 August 1942 the border was closed. People fleeing only on “racial grounds” did not count as political refugees.
30348.m: In August 1942 Switzerland closed the border to Jewish refugees.

30349.q: Why did many Jewish people flee Germany from 1933?
a: They were persecuted by the Nazis
They were looking for farm work
They wanted to go on holiday
They had to join the army
30349.e: The Nazis took away Jewish people's rights, their property and later their lives. Many tried to flee abroad, including to Switzerland.
30349.m: Jewish people fled persecution by the Nazis.

30350.q: What did the Bergier Commission investigate in the 1990s?
a: Switzerland's role in the Second World War
The building of the Gotthard Tunnel
30350.e: Historians examined Switzerland's refugee policy and business dealings during the Second World War. They criticised the fact that many persecuted people had been turned away.
30350.m: The Bergier Commission investigated Switzerland in the Second World War.

30351.q: What did the Federal Council publicly apologise for in 1995?
30351.e: On the 50th anniversary of the end of the war, President Kaspar Villiger apologised for the J stamp. Switzerland had agreed on it with Germany in 1938.
30351.m: In 1995 the Federal Council apologised for the J stamp.

30352.q: How many people found protection in Switzerland for shorter or longer periods during the Second World War?
30352.e: They included civilian refugees, interned soldiers and children on recovery holidays. At the same time, however, many persecuted people were turned away at the border.
30352.m: In the Second World War almost 300,000 people found protection in Switzerland.

30353.q: What job did Paul Grüninger have when he helped Jewish refugees in 1938?
30353.e: Grüninger commanded the St Gallen cantonal police. At the border with Austria he decided whether many refugees could enter.
30353.m: Paul Grüninger was police commander in St Gallen.

30354.q: According to what we know today, how many refugees did Paul Grüninger save?
30354.e: In 1938 and 1939 he let several hundred Jewish refugees enter. Without him they would have been sent back.
30354.m: Paul Grüninger saved the lives of several hundred people.

30355.q: What happened to Paul Grüninger in 1939 after his help became known?
30355.e: Grüninger lost his job and his pension in 1939. In 1940 he was convicted of breach of official duty and then lived in poverty.
30355.m: Paul Grüninger was dismissed for his help.

30356.q: Which honour did Paul Grüninger receive from the Yad Vashem memorial in 1971?
30356.e: Yad Vashem in Jerusalem honours people who saved Jews at the risk of their lives or at great personal cost. Grüninger received this title in 1971.
30356.m: Paul Grüninger is one of the Righteous Among the Nations.

30357.q: How was Paul Grüninger honoured after his death?
30357.e: Grüninger died in poverty in 1972. In 1995 a court acquitted him, and today he is honoured as a rescuer of refugees.
30357.m: Paul Grüninger's name was cleared after his death.

30358.q: What in St Gallen has carried Paul Grüninger's name since 2006?
30358.e: FC Brühl's stadium has been called the Paul Grüninger Stadium since 2006. Grüninger himself had played football for FC Brühl.
30358.m: In St Gallen a stadium remembers Paul Grüninger.

30359.q: From which country did most of the refugees Paul Grüninger helped in 1938 flee?
30359.e: After Austria was annexed by the German Reich in March 1938, many Jews fled to Switzerland. Near St Gallen they tried to get across the Rhine.
30359.m: Grüninger mainly helped refugees from Austria.

30360.q: In which city did the Swiss diplomat Carl Lutz save Jews from deportation?
30360.e: From 1942 Carl Lutz was vice-consul at the Swiss legation in Budapest. In 1944 the deportations of Hungarian Jews began there.
30360.m: Carl Lutz saved thousands of Jews in Budapest.

30361.q: With which documents did Carl Lutz protect the Jews in Budapest?
30361.e: Lutz issued letters of protection that placed their holders under Swiss protection. The authorities often respected them and did not deport these people.
30361.m: Carl Lutz saved people with letters of protection.

30362.q: What was the building in Budapest called where Carl Lutz sheltered persecuted Jews?
30362.e: The “Glass House” had been the headquarters of a glass company, and the Swiss mission used it in 1944. Thousands of people found refuge there.
30362.m: Thousands found protection in the Glass House in Budapest.

30363.q: Roughly how many people did Carl Lutz help in Budapest?
30363.e: With letters of protection and safe houses, Carl Lutz saved tens of thousands of Jews. It ranks among the biggest rescue operations of the Second World War.
30363.m: Carl Lutz saved tens of thousands of people.

30364.q: Why is Carl Lutz honoured as a hero today?
a: He saved many Jews from death
30364.e: In 1944 in Budapest Carl Lutz protected many Jews from deportation. Later other diplomats such as Raoul Wallenberg copied his method.
30364.m: Carl Lutz is honoured for saving many Jews.

30365.q: How did the Swiss authorities first react to Carl Lutz's rescue operation after the war?
a: They criticised him for overstepping his authority
They elected him to the Federal Council
They gave him a monument in Bern
30365.e: The authorities saw part of his independent action as overstepping his authority. Only in 1995 did Switzerland clear his name after his death.
30365.m: Carl Lutz received recognition for his deeds in Switzerland only late.

30366.q: During which war did Carl Lutz save people in Budapest?
30366.e: Carl Lutz worked in Budapest from 1942 to 1945. In 1944 the deportations of Hungarian Jews began there.
30366.m: Carl Lutz helped people in Budapest in the Second World War.

30367.q: What does the abbreviation AHV stand for?
30367.e: AHV stands for old-age and survivors' insurance. It pays pensions to retired people and to surviving dependants such as widows and orphans.
30367.m: AHV protects old people and surviving dependants.

30368.q: Which pillar of the pension system is AHV?
30368.e: Switzerland has three pillars: AHV (1st pillar), pension fund (2nd pillar) and private savings (3rd pillar). AHV is meant to cover basic living costs.
30368.m: AHV is the first pillar of the pension system.

30369.q: What did the “magic formula” in Switzerland settle?
a: How the Federal Council seats are shared among the parties
30369.e: From 1959 the four biggest parties shared the seven seats on the Federal Council according to a fixed formula.
30369.m: The magic formula shared out the Federal Council seats among the big parties.

30370.q: Which party got a second seat on the Federal Council with the magic formula in 1959?
30370.e: In 1959 two Social Democrats, including Hans-Peter Tschudi, were elected. This gave the SP two seats for the first time.
30370.m: Since 1959 the SP has had two Federal Council seats.

30371.q: What is the principle called that all the big parties sit in government together?
30371.e: In concordance, the main parties share responsibility for government. The magic formula counted as the best-known form of this concordance.
30371.m: Concordance means the big parties govern together.

30372.q: Which event ended the 1959 magic formula in 2003?
a: The election of Christoph Blocher to the Federal Council
The introduction of women's right to vote
The resignation of all SP Federal Councillors
The founding of the canton of Jura
30372.e: In 2003 Christoph Blocher (SVP) was elected and Ruth Metzler (CVP) voted out. From then on the SVP had two seats and the CVP only one.
30372.m: The old magic formula ended with Blocher's election in 2003.

30373.q: What took place all over Switzerland on 14 June 1991?
a: The opening of the Federal Palace
The founding of the first women's party
30373.e: On 14 June 1991 hundreds of thousands of women stopped work. They demanded that equality between women and men finally be put into practice.
30373.m: On 14 June 1991 women went on strike for equality.

30374.q: What were foreign workers called who were only allowed to work in Switzerland for a few months a year?
30374.e: Seasonal workers got a permit for one season, for example in building, hotels and restaurants, or farming. After that they had to leave Switzerland.
30374.m: Seasonal workers only worked in Switzerland during one season.

30375.q: Which country did most seasonal workers come from in the 1950s and 1960s?
30375.e: In 1948 Switzerland signed a recruitment agreement with Italy. In the post-war years especially many workers came from Italy, later also from Spain, Portugal and Yugoslavia.
30375.m: Most of the early seasonal workers came from Italy.

30377.q: In which sectors did seasonal workers work especially often?
a: Watch sales and the stock exchange
30377.e: These sectors need many workers depending on the season. On building sites and in hotels there was especially a lot of work in summer.
30377.m: Seasonal workers often worked on building sites and in hotels.

30378.q: In which year did Switzerland vote on the Schwarzenbach initiative?
30378.e: The vote took place on 7 June 1970. At that time only men were allowed to vote.
30378.m: The Schwarzenbach initiative went to the vote in 1970.

30379.q: What did the Schwarzenbach initiative of 1970 want to limit?
30379.e: James Schwarzenbach's initiative wanted to cut the proportion of foreigners in almost all cantons to no more than 10 per cent. The people and the cantons rejected it.
30379.m: The Schwarzenbach initiative wanted fewer foreigners in Switzerland.

30381.q: What stood out particularly in the vote on the Schwarzenbach initiative?
a: That it took place twice on the same day
30381.e: Turnout reached its highest level since 1947. This shows how strongly the issue moved the population.
30381.m: The Schwarzenbach initiative got very many voters to the polls.

30382.q: In which year did the secret files scandal (Fichenskandal) come to light?
30382.e: At the end of 1989 a parliamentary inquiry published its report. It had discovered that the state had kept watch on hundreds of thousands of people.
30382.m: The secret files scandal became known in 1989.

a: An index card with notes about a person
30383.e: Fiche is the French word for index card. On the fiches, the police noted observations about people and organisations.
30383.m: A fiche is an index card with surveillance notes.

30384.q: Roughly how many fiches had been created by 1990?
30384.e: By 1990 the federal government and the cantons had created about 900,000 fiches. They covered over 700,000 people and organisations.

30385.q: What could many people ask for after the secret files scandal?
a: Money from the state for each fiche
30385.e: Over 300,000 people wanted to know what the state had noted about them. They could look at their fiche, often with parts blacked out.
30385.m: After the scandal you could see your own fiche.

30386.q: Which resignation led to the inquiry in which the secret files scandal came to light?
a: The resignation of Federal Councillor Elisabeth Kopp
The resignation of Federal Councillor Walther Stampfli
The resignation of the whole government
The resignation of the head of Swissair
30386.e: Elisabeth Kopp resigned because she had warned her husband about an investigation. The parliamentary inquiry then examined the Justice Department and came across the fiches.
30386.m: The Kopp affair led to the discovery of the fiches.

30387.q: During which period were most people put on file because communists were feared?
30387.e: In the Cold War, anything that looked like left-wing politics counted as suspicious. Trade unionists, peace activists and foreigners, for example, were watched.
30387.m: The fiches came about mainly out of fear of communism.

30388.q: What happened in Bern on 3 March 1990?
a: A big demonstration against the snooping state
The election of the first woman Federal Councillor
The signing of the bilateral agreements
30388.e: About 30,000 people demonstrated in Bern against the surveillance. Afterwards many asked to see their own fiche.
30388.m: In 1990 thousands protested in Bern against the snooping state.

30389.q: What does the abbreviation EEA stand for?
30389.e: EEA stands for European Economic Area. It links the EU's single market with some EFTA states.
30389.m: EEA stands for European Economic Area.

30390.q: On which day did Switzerland reject joining the EEA?
30390.e: On 6 December 1992 the people and the cantons said no to the EEA. The day counts among the most important in recent Swiss history.
30390.m: On 6 December 1992 Switzerland said no to the EEA.

30391.q: Which politician led the campaign against joining the EEA?
30391.e: Christoph Blocher, SVP National Councillor from Zurich, became the best-known opponent. The vote made him famous across the country.
30391.m: Christoph Blocher led the opposition to the EEA.

30392.q: How many agreements make up the Bilateral Agreements I?
30392.e: The Bilateral Agreements I consist of seven agreements, for example on the free movement of persons, land transport and research. They were signed in 1999.
30392.m: The Bilateral Agreements I consist of seven agreements.

30393.q: How did the people decide on the Bilateral Agreements I in 2000?
a: They were not allowed to vote
30393.e: On 21 May 2000 about 67 per cent said yes to the Bilateral Agreements I. They came into force in 2002.
30393.m: The people clearly accepted the Bilateral Agreements I in 2000.

30394.q: What does the so-called guillotine clause of the Bilateral Agreements I do?
a: If one agreement ends, all seven end
Each agreement expires after one year
The EU may change Swiss laws
Only one agreement applies for ever
30394.e: The seven agreements are linked together. If one side cancels one of them, the others also become invalid.
30394.m: The guillotine clause links all the Bilateral Agreements I together.

30395.q: Which agreement of the Bilateral Agreements I allows EU citizens to work and live in Switzerland?
a: The Agreement on the Free Movement of Persons
30395.e: Free movement of persons allows citizens of Switzerland and the EU to live and work in each other's territory. It is the best known of the seven agreements.
30395.m: Free movement of persons allows people to live and work freely.

30396.q: Which popular initiative of 2014 called the free movement of persons into question?
30396.e: On 9 February 2014 the people narrowly accepted the mass immigration initiative. It demanded that Switzerland control immigration itself.
30396.m: The mass immigration initiative of 2014 concerned immigration.

30397.q: What did the Federal Council decide about the framework agreement with the EU in May 2021?
a: It signed the agreement at once
It cancelled all the bilateral agreements
30397.e: In May 2021 the Federal Council ended the negotiations on the institutional framework agreement. After that, new talks began on a package of treaties.
30397.m: In 2021 the Federal Council broke off the negotiations on the framework agreement.

30398.q: On which day did all Swissair planes stay on the ground?
30398.e: On 2 October 2001 Swissair had to stop all its flights. This event is called the grounding.
30398.m: The Swissair grounding happened on 2 October 2001.

30399.q: Why could the Swissair planes no longer take off on 2 October 2001?
a: The company could no longer pay for fuel
The pilots went on strike for more pay
30399.e: Swissair had huge debts and no money left. Suppliers demanded cash payment and stopped refuelling the planes.
30399.m: Swissair ran out of money in 2001.

30400.q: What did Swissair buy in large numbers before the grounding?
30400.e: Swissair bought shares in many airlines, most of them small. These made heavy losses and helped cause the collapse.
30400.m: Expensive purchases of other airlines drove Swissair into debt.

30401.q: Which nickname showed how rich Swissair was in the 1980s?
30401.e: Swissair had so much money in reserve that people called it the “flying bank”. That made the shock of the grounding all the greater.
30401.m: Swissair used to be seen as a flying bank.

30402.q: Which group took over the airline Swiss in 2005?
30402.e: The German airline Lufthansa took over Swiss from 2005. But Swiss still flies under its own name.
30402.m: Swiss has belonged to Lufthansa since 2005.

30403.q: What is the assembly called in which all UN members are represented?
30403.e: In the General Assembly every member has one vote. It admitted Switzerland in New York in 2002.
30403.m: In the UN General Assembly every country has one vote.

30404.q: What does the Schengen Agreement abolish at the borders?
a: The need to have a passport
30404.e: In the Schengen Area, people are no longer systematically checked at the internal borders. But spot checks are still possible.
30404.m: Schengen abolishes systematic checks on people at the borders.

30405.q: How did the Swiss people vote on joining Schengen in 2005?
30405.e: On 5 June 2005, 54.6 per cent voted yes to Schengen and Dublin. The agreement is part of the Bilateral Agreements II.

30406.q: Do you still need to carry a passport or identity card when travelling in the Schengen Area?
a: Yes, because checks are still possible
No, ID documents have been abolished
30406.e: There are no longer systematic checks at the borders, but there are still spot checks. That is why you always need a valid ID.
30406.m: You need ID even in the Schengen Area.

30407.q: Why are there still customs checks at the Swiss border despite Schengen?
a: Because Switzerland is not part of the EU customs union
Because Schengen only applies to aeroplanes
Because customs duties must be in the constitution
30407.e: Schengen only concerns checks on people. As Switzerland is not in the EU customs union, goods are still checked.
30407.m: Despite Schengen, customs still check goods.

30408.q: Where does the Schengen Agreement get its name from?
30408.e: The agreement was signed in 1985 in the wine-growing village of Schengen in Luxembourg. The village lies near the borders with Germany and France.
30408.m: Schengen is a village in Luxembourg.

30409.q: What is the Dublin Agreement, which applies together with Schengen, about?
a: Which country is responsible for asylum applications
30409.e: Dublin sets out which country has to examine an asylum application. Usually it is the country a person entered first.
30409.m: Dublin decides who is responsible for asylum applications.

30410.q: What is the shared police search database of the Schengen countries called?
30410.e: In the Schengen Information System (SIS), police forces share information on wanted people and objects. It replaces part of the old border checks.
30410.m: The Schengen Information System helps the police find wanted people.

30411.e: Expo.02 was Switzerland’s sixth national exhibition. It took place in 2002.

30412.q: In which region did Expo.02 take place?
30412.e: Expo.02 took place around Lake Biel, Lake Neuchâtel and Lake Murten. This area is called the Three Lakes region.
30412.m: Expo.02 took place in the Three Lakes region.

30413.q: What were the exhibition sites of Expo.02 called?
30413.e: The four exhibition sites on the lake shores were called Arteplages. They were in Biel, Neuchâtel, Murten and Yverdon-les-Bains; there was also a floating Arteplage of the canton of Jura.
30413.m: The exhibition sites of Expo.02 were called Arteplages.

30414.q: Which town was NOT the site of an Arteplage at Expo.02?
30414.e: The Arteplages were in Biel, Neuchâtel, Murten and Yverdon-les-Bains. Bern was not an exhibition site.
30414.m: Bern had no Arteplage at Expo.02.

30415.q: What was the “Monolith” in Lake Murten at Expo.02?
30415.e: The Monolith was a large, rusty steel cube floating in Lake Murten. It was one of the best-known structures of Expo.02.
30415.m: The Monolith was a steel cube in Lake Murten.

30416.q: Under which name was the national exhibition originally planned?
30416.e: The exhibition was first planned for 2001. Because of problems with the planning, it was postponed by a year.
30416.m: Expo.02 was originally going to be called Expo.01.

30417.q: Roughly how many visits did Expo.02 count?
30417.e: Expo.02 counted 10.3 million visits. The record day was the last day of the exhibition, 20 October 2002.
30417.m: Expo.02 had around ten million visits.

30418.q: Roughly how long is the Gotthard Base Tunnel?
30418.e: The Gotthard Base Tunnel is about 57 kilometres long. That makes it the longest railway tunnel in the world.
30418.m: The Gotthard Base Tunnel is about 57 kilometres long.

30419.q: Which two cantons does the Gotthard Base Tunnel connect?
30419.e: The north portal is in Erstfeld in the canton of Uri, the south portal in Bodio in Ticino.
30419.m: The Gotthard Base Tunnel connects Uri and Ticino.

30420.q: Which major rail project does the Gotthard Base Tunnel belong to?
30420.e: NRLA stands for New Rail Link through the Alps (in German NEAT). It also includes the Lötschberg and Ceneri base tunnels.
30420.m: The Gotthard Base Tunnel is the centrepiece of the NRLA.

30421.q: How many tubes does the Gotthard Base Tunnel have?
a: Two tubes with one track each
Three tubes with two tracks each
Four tubes with one track each
30421.e: The tunnel has two single-track tubes about 40 metres apart. They are linked at regular intervals by cross-passages.
30421.m: The Gotthard Base Tunnel has two single-track tubes.

30422.q: What was mainly used to dig the Gotthard Base Tunnel?
30422.e: Big tunnel boring machines ate their way through the rock. In October 2010 one of them broke through the last metres of rock.
30422.m: The base tunnel was built with tunnel boring machines.

30423.q: What is the Gotthard Base Tunnel mainly meant to achieve?
a: More freight by rail instead of by road
30423.e: Flat base tunnels allow long, heavy freight trains. This is meant to move more freight through the Alps onto the railway.
30423.m: The base tunnel moves freight from road to rail.

30424.q: Where, for example, can you find your AHV (old-age insurance) number?
30424.e: Everyone in Switzerland has an AHV number, children too. It is printed, for example, on the health insurance card.
30424.m: The AHV number is on the health insurance card.

30425.q: What did the “AHV 21” reform change about the retirement age for women?
a: It rises step by step from 64 to 65
30425.e: With AHV 21, the retirement age for women is being raised step by step to 65. That makes it the same as for men.
30425.m: With AHV 21, women and men receive their pension at 65.

30426.q: Whom does the invalidity insurance (IV) help?
a: People who cannot work fully because of illness or disability
30426.e: The IV has existed since 1960. It supports people who can no longer work fully because of an illness or disability.
30426.m: The IV helps people with an illness or disability.

30427.q: Do all pensioners receive the same AHV pension?
a: No, the highest is twice as much as the lowest
Yes, everyone gets exactly the same
No, rich people get ten times more
No, only men get a pension
30427.e: The pension depends on income and years of contributions. But the maximum pension is only twice as high as the minimum pension.
30427.m: The largest AHV pension is twice as high as the smallest.

30428.q: What do pensioners receive if their AHV pension is not enough to live on?
a: A tax bonus from the municipality
30428.e: Supplementary benefits help when pension and income do not cover the cost of living. They have been paid since 1966.
30428.m: Supplementary benefits help when the pension is not enough.

30429.q: What is the money that working people pay into the AHV today used for?
a: For each person’s own savings account
30429.e: The AHV passes the money straight on: the contributions of working people pay the pensions of today’s retired people.
30429.m: Working people’s contributions pay today’s AHV pensions.

30430.q: Roughly how long did the magic formula of 1959 last?
30430.e: The magic formula for sharing the Federal Council seats lasted from 1959 to 2003, so 44 years. Then the SVP got a second seat.
30430.m: The magic formula lasted over 40 years.

30431.q: Since 1971, what has the BGB, which had a Federal Council seat under the magic formula, been called?
30431.e: In 1971 the Farmers’, Traders’ and Citizens’ Party (BGB) merged with other parties to form the Swiss People’s Party. Since then it has been called the SVP.
30431.m: In 1971 the BGB became the SVP.

30433.q: What did the women in the Valais village of Unterbäch do in 1957?
a: They took part in a vote as a symbolic act
They elected a female Federal Councillor
They went on strike for a week
30433.e: In 1957 the municipality let the women take part in a federal vote. Their votes did not officially count, but the action became famous.
30433.m: In Unterbäch in 1957, women voted for the first time as a symbolic act.

30434.q: What did the voters accept on 14 June 1981?
a: The equality article in the constitution
30434.e: Since 1981 the Federal Constitution has stated that men and women have equal rights. It also requires equal pay for work of equal value.
30434.m: Since 1981 equality has been part of the constitution.

30435.q: What was the big demonstration for women’s suffrage on 1 March 1969 called?
30435.e: In 1969 around 5,000 women and men marched to the Federal Palace. The demonstration increased the pressure to introduce women’s suffrage quickly.
30435.m: The March on Bern in 1969 demanded votes for women.

30436.q: Since when have women been able to be elected to the National Council?
30436.e: With women’s suffrage in 1971, women could also be elected. In the same year, the first female National Councillors entered the Federal Palace.
30436.m: Women have sat in the National Council since 1971.

30437.q: Who was allowed to vote at federal level in Switzerland before 1971?
30437.e: Until 1971 only men had the right to vote and be elected at federal level. Women fought for it for decades.
30437.m: Before 1971 only men were allowed to vote.

30438.q: Which neighbouring country introduced women’s suffrage only in 1984, even later than Switzerland?
30438.e: Liechtenstein introduced women’s suffrage in 1984, the last country in Europe to do so. Switzerland in 1971 was also one of the last.
30438.m: Liechtenstein only introduced votes for women in 1984.

30439.q: In which year did the second big women’s strike take place in Switzerland?
30439.e: On 14 June 2019 hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets. As in the first women’s strike, they demanded real equality, for example in pay.
30439.m: The second big women’s strike took place in 2019.

30440.q: Which church principality did the Jura region belong to until the French Revolution?
30440.e: For centuries the Jura was part of the Prince-Bishopric of Basel. The Bishop of Basel ruled the area as a worldly prince.
30440.m: The Jura used to belong to the Prince-Bishopric of Basel.

30441.q: Why did the Bishop of Basel leave the city of Basel after the Reformation and move to the Jura?
a: Because the climate was better in the Jura
30441.e: Basel became Protestant in 1529. The Catholic bishop moved to Porrentruy and lived in the castle there.
30441.m: After the Reformation, the prince-bishops of Basel lived in Porrentruy.

30442.q: Which breed of horse comes from the canton of Jura?
30442.e: The Franches-Montagnes is considered the last native Swiss horse breed. It is named after the Franches-Montagnes area (Freiberge in German).
30442.m: The Franches-Montagnes is a horse from the Jura.

30443.q: What is the centre of attention every year at the Marché-Concours in Saignelégier?
30443.e: At the Marché-Concours in August, Franches-Montagnes horses are shown and there are horse races. It is a big festival of the Franches-Montagnes region.
30443.m: The Marché-Concours is the horse festival in Saignelégier.

30444.q: Which language does the large majority speak in the canton of Jura?
30444.e: The canton of Jura is French-speaking. Only the small municipality of Ederswiler is German-speaking.
30444.m: People in the canton of Jura speak French.

30445.q: What did the Jura separatists want?
30445.e: The separatists wanted to separate the northern Jura from the canton of Bern. Their youth group, the Béliers, drew attention with their actions. The canton of Jura was created in 1979.
30445.m: The separatists fought for a separate canton of Jura.

30446.q: Which river flows through the little town of Saint-Ursanne in the canton of Jura?
30446.e: In the Jura, the Doubs makes a big loop through Switzerland. The bridge over the Doubs at Saint-Ursanne is a popular photo spot.

30447.q: What were seasonal workers (Saisonniers) not allowed to do in Switzerland?
a: Bring their families to live with them
30447.e: Seasonal workers were not allowed to bring their families. Husbands, wives and children usually had to stay in their home country.
30447.m: Seasonal workers were not allowed to bring their families to Switzerland.

30448.q: What did many children of seasonal workers who came to Switzerland secretly have to go through?
a: They lived in hiding and could not be noticed
They had to serve in the army
They went to special seasonal workers’ schools
They got a Swiss passport straight away
30448.e: Because families were not allowed to join the workers, thousands of children lived hidden in flats. Often they could neither play outside nor go to school.
30448.m: Many children of seasonal workers lived in hiding.

30449.q: What did seasonal workers often have to do when entering Switzerland?
30449.e: Seasonal workers were given a medical examination at the border. Anyone considered ill was sent back.
30449.m: Seasonal workers were medically examined at the border.

30451.q: Which slogan did the supporters of the Schwarzenbach initiative use?
30451.e: The supporters spoke of Switzerland being “overrun by foreigners” (“Überfremdung”). The word had a strong influence on politics in the 1960s and 1970s.

30452.q: What did business and the Federal Council fear if the Schwarzenbach initiative were accepted?
a: That many businesses would have to close
That wages would double at once
That Switzerland would have to join the EU
That the AHV would be abolished
30452.e: Without foreign workers, many companies could not have carried on. People feared that businesses would close and jobs would be lost.
30452.m: Business feared that companies would have to close.

30453.q: Which part of the country mostly voted for the EEA in 1992?
30453.e: Geneva, Vaud, Neuchâtel, Jura and Fribourg said yes, as did the two Basels. The rest of German-speaking Switzerland and Ticino said no.
30453.m: In the EEA vote, it was mainly French-speaking Switzerland that said yes.

30454.q: Which neighbouring country of Switzerland is in the EEA but not in the EU?
30454.e: Liechtenstein joined the EEA in 1995 but is not an EU member. Switzerland is in neither the EEA nor the EU.
30454.m: Liechtenstein is in the EEA, Switzerland is not.

30455.q: After the no to the EEA, how does Switzerland mainly organise its relations with the EU?
a: As a member of the EU
With the euro as its currency
30455.e: After the no in 1992, Switzerland made separate agreements with the EU, the Bilaterals. They cover things such as trade and travel.
30455.m: Switzerland organises its relations with the EU through bilateral agreements.

30456.q: What was unusually high in the EEA vote of 1992?
30456.e: Almost 79 per cent of those entitled to vote took part. That has rarely happened in a vote.
30456.m: Almost 79 per cent took part in the EEA vote.

30457.q: With whom did Switzerland make the Bilateral Agreements?
30457.e: The Bilateral Agreements set out relations between Switzerland and the EU. There are the Bilaterals I from 1999 and the Bilaterals II from 2004.
30457.m: The Bilaterals are agreements between Switzerland and the EU.

30458.q: What is the title of the person who runs the UN’s administration?
30458.e: The Secretary-General runs the UN’s administration and represents it around the world.
30458.m: The UN is led by a Secretary-General.

30459.q: Roughly how many countries are members of the UN?
30459.e: Today 193 countries belong to the UN. Switzerland has been a member since 2002.
30459.m: Almost every country in the world is in the UN.

30460.q: In which city does the UN have its headquarters?
30460.e: The headquarters of the United Nations is in New York. The General Assembly also meets there.
30460.m: The UN has its headquarters in New York.

30461.q: Which organisation that came before the UN had Switzerland already joined in 1920?
30461.e: Switzerland joined the League of Nations in 1920 after a referendum. Its headquarters were in Geneva.
30461.m: Switzerland was in the League of Nations from 1920.

30462.q: Which UN body was founded in 2006 and meets in Geneva?
30462.e: The UN Human Rights Council was created in 2006 and is based in Geneva. Switzerland had campaigned hard for it.
30462.m: The UN Human Rights Council meets in Geneva.

30463.q: What could many travellers not do on the day of the Swissair grounding?
a: Take off on the flight they had booked
30463.e: All Swissair planes stayed on the ground. Thousands of passengers were stuck at airports all over the world.
30463.m: During the grounding, all Swissair flights were cancelled.

30464.q: Which regional airline did the new Swiss build on in 2002?
30464.e: Crossair from Basel was a subsidiary of Swissair. It was renamed and took over Swissair’s most important routes.

30465.q: Which other NRLA base tunnel opened as early as 2007?
30465.e: The Lötschberg Base Tunnel between Frutigen and Raron went into service in 2007. It was the first completed base tunnel of the NRLA.
30465.m: The Lötschberg Base Tunnel opened in 2007.

30809.q: Which animal is thought to be humans' oldest domestic animal?
30809.e: The dog was domesticated from the wolf by Ice Age hunter-gatherers. Sheep, goats, cattle and pigs only followed when people settled down.
30809.m: The dog is the oldest domestic animal.

32803.q: Which famous dog breed is linked to the hospice on the Great St Bernard Pass?
32803.e: Since the 17th century, the canons of the hospice kept large dogs that helped search for lost travellers. This led to the St Bernard breed.
32803.m: The St Bernard comes from the hospice on the Great St Bernard Pass.

50401.q: Which filled chocolate sweet was invented in Belgium?
50401.e: The praline was invented in Belgium in 1912. It is made of a chocolate shell with a soft filling.
50401.m: The praline was invented in Belgium.

50402.q: What colours is the flag of Belgium?
50402.e: The Belgian flag has three vertical stripes in black, yellow and red. The colours come from old coats of arms of the country.
50402.m: The flag of Belgium is black, yellow and red.

50403.q: Which country do the Smurfs come from?
50403.e: The little blue Smurfs were created by the Belgian artist Peyo. They first appeared in a comic in 1958.

50404.q: Who is at the head of the country of Belgium?
50404.e: Belgium is a kingdom. Philippe has been King of the Belgians since 2013 (as of 2025).
50404.m: Belgium is led by a king.

50405.q: Which Belgian city is famous for trading diamonds?
50405.e: Diamonds have been traded and cut in Antwerp for centuries. The city also has a large port.
50405.m: Antwerp is the city of diamonds.

50406.q: Which country is a neighbour of Belgium?
50406.e: Belgium borders France, Germany, Luxembourg and the Netherlands. To the north lies the North Sea.
50406.m: France is a neighbour of Belgium.

50407.q: What is the capital of Belgium?
50407.e: Brussels is the capital of Belgium. The king and his family also live there.
50407.m: Brussels is the capital of Belgium.

50408.q: What is the name of the small fountain statue of a boy that is very famous in Brussels?
50408.e: Manneken Pis is a bronze statue of a boy weeing, only about 60 centimetres tall. He owns more than 900 costumes, which he wears in turn.
50408.m: Manneken Pis is a famous statue in Brussels.

50409.q: Which building in Brussels is made of huge shiny balls?
50409.e: The Atomium was built in 1958 for a world fair. It shows a tiny building block of iron enlarged many billions of times.
50409.m: The Atomium in Brussels is made of big balls.

50410.q: Every two years a huge carpet lies on the big square in Brussels. What is it made of?
50410.e: Every two years in August, a carpet made of many thousands of flowers lies on the Grand-Place in Brussels.
50410.m: Brussels has a flower carpet every two years.

50411.q: Which group of countries has important buildings in Brussels?
50411.e: Important parts of the European Union work in Brussels, for example the European Commission. The Olympic Committee, FIFA and the Red Cross, on the other hand, have their headquarters in Switzerland.
50411.m: The European Union works in Brussels.

50412.q: Which two languages are official languages in Brussels?
50412.e: In Brussels, street signs are usually in two languages, French and Dutch. In everyday life you hear French the most.
50412.m: In Brussels people speak French and Dutch.

50413.q: What is painted on many house walls in Brussels?
50413.e: Brussels is known as the city of comics. Big pictures of famous comic characters are painted on many house walls.
50413.m: In Brussels you can see comic pictures on many house walls.

50414.q: What can you see in the Mini-Europe park in Brussels?
50414.e: In the Mini-Europe park, many well-known buildings from Europe stand as small models. Swissminiatur in Ticino is a similar park.
50414.m: Mini-Europe shows Europe's buildings in miniature.

50415.q: In which city does the government of the Netherlands work?
50415.e: The government and parliament of the Netherlands are based in The Hague. The king also lives there.
50415.m: The government of the Netherlands works in The Hague.

50416.q: What do many people call the Netherlands, even though it is only part of the country?
50416.e: Holland is really only a region in the west of the country with two provinces. Even so, many people say “Holland” for the whole country.
50416.m: Holland is only part of the Netherlands.

50417.q: Which language is spoken in the Netherlands?
50417.e: People in the Netherlands speak Dutch. It is related to German, so some words sound similar.
50417.m: Dutch is spoken in the Netherlands.

50418.q: What is special about many areas of the Netherlands?
a: They lie lower than the sea
50418.e: About a quarter of the country lies below sea level. Without protection, the sea would flood the land there.
50418.m: Many areas of the Netherlands lie lower than the sea.

50419.q: What protects the land in the Netherlands from the sea?
50419.e: Dykes are long, high banks of earth along the coast and the rivers. They keep the water away from the land.
50419.m: Dykes protect the Netherlands from the sea.

50420.q: Which means of transport do people in the Netherlands use especially often?
50420.e: There are more bicycles than people in the Netherlands. The country is flat and has a great many cycle paths.
50420.m: Lots of people in the Netherlands ride bicycles.

50421.q: What colour do Dutch fans wear at sports events?
50421.e: Orange is the colour of the royal family, which is called the “House of Orange”. That is why fans of the Netherlands wear orange.
50421.m: Fans of the Netherlands wear orange.

50422.q: Which kind of cheese is named after a town in the Netherlands?
50422.e: Gouda is a town in the Netherlands whose market has traded cheese for a long time. Emmental, on the other hand, comes from Switzerland.
50422.m: Gouda is a cheese from the Netherlands.

50423.q: What are the traditional Dutch shoes, called klompen, made of?
50423.e: Klompen are carved from a single piece of wood. In the past, farmers wore them for work in wet fields.

50424.q: What do the old houses along the canals in Amsterdam often look like?
50424.e: It is often said that taxes used to depend on how wide a house was along the canal. So houses were built narrow, but tall and deep.
50424.m: The old canal houses are narrow and tall.

50425.q: What are the grachten in Amsterdam?
50425.e: Grachten are canals that run like rings through the old town. In the past, ships carried goods along them right up to the houses.

50426.q: Roughly how many bridges are there in Amsterdam?
50426.e: Because there are so many canals, Amsterdam needs a great many bridges. There are well over 1,000.

50427.q: What do some people live on in the canals of Amsterdam?
50427.e: There are around 2,500 houseboats on the canals. People live in them just like in a flat.
50427.m: Some people in Amsterdam live on houseboats.

50428.q: Whose hiding place can you visit in a museum in Amsterdam?
50428.e: Anne Frank was a Jewish girl who had to hide with her family in a back building during the Second World War. There she wrote her famous diary.
50428.m: In Amsterdam you can visit Anne Frank's hiding place.

50429.q: Which painter is a famous museum in Amsterdam named after?
50429.e: The Van Gogh Museum has many of the painter's pictures, for example his sunflowers. He came from the Netherlands.
50429.m: Amsterdam has a museum for Vincent van Gogh.

50430.q: Which painter painted the large picture “The Night Watch”, which hangs in Amsterdam?
50430.e: Rembrandt was a famous painter from the Netherlands. “The Night Watch” hangs in the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam.

50431.q: What is the hook at the top of many old houses in Amsterdam for?
50431.e: The stairs in the old houses are very steep. So large furniture is pulled up the outside with a rope on the hook and brought in through the window.
50431.m: The hook on the house is used to lift furniture.

50432.q: Which river is Amsterdam named after?
50432.e: The city grew up at a dam on the River Amstel. That is why it is called Amsterdam.
50432.m: Amsterdam is named after the River Amstel.

50433.q: What were many windmills in the Netherlands used for?
50433.e: Many mills pumped water from the low land into the canals. This kept fields and villages dry.
50433.m: Windmills in the Netherlands pumped water away.

50434.q: What did windmills often grind in the past?
50434.e: Heavy millstones turned in many windmills. They ground grain into flour for bread.

50435.q: At which place in the Netherlands do 19 old windmills stand close together?
50435.e: In Kinderdijk, 19 old windmills stand along canals. They have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1997.
50435.m: There are 19 old windmills at Kinderdijk.

50436.q: How many sails does a typical windmill in the Netherlands have?
50436.e: Most old windmills have four large sails. The wind turns them and so drives the mill.
50436.m: A typical windmill has four sails.

50437.q: What do modern wind turbines produce?
50437.e: Modern wind turbines turn a generator that produces electricity. There are also some wind turbines in Switzerland, for example in the Jura.

50438.q: What does a tulip grow from?
50438.e: Tulips grow from flower bulbs that are planted in the ground in autumn. Food for the plant is stored in the bulb.
50438.m: A tulip grows from a bulb.

50439.q: In which season do tulips flower?
50439.e: Tulips are among the first colourful flowers of the year. They usually flower in April and May.

50440.q: What is the name of the famous flower park in the Netherlands with millions of tulips?
50440.e: Every spring, millions of flowers bloom at Keukenhof, mostly tulips. The park is only open for a few weeks a year.
50440.m: Keukenhof is a famous tulip park.

50441.q: What was going on with tulip bulbs in Holland almost 400 years ago?
50441.e: Around 1637, rare tulip bulbs were so sought after that some cost more than a house. This is called “tulip mania”.
50441.m: Tulip bulbs used to be very expensive in Holland.

50442.q: What is the capital of Luxembourg?
50442.e: The capital has the same name as the country. The city of Luxembourg sits on rocks above deep valleys.
50442.m: The capital of Luxembourg is also called Luxembourg.

50443.q: What kind of country is Luxembourg?
50443.e: Luxembourg is the only grand duchy in the world. A grand duke is at its head.

50444.q: Which language of their own do people in Luxembourg speak with each other?
50444.e: Luxembourgers speak Luxembourgish with each other. French and German are also official languages.
50444.m: Luxembourgish is the language of the Luxembourgers.

50445.q: How big is Luxembourg compared with Switzerland?
50445.e: Luxembourg is about 16 times smaller than Switzerland. It is roughly the size of the canton of Ticino.
50445.m: Luxembourg is much smaller than Switzerland.

50446.q: Which country is NOT a neighbour of Luxembourg?
50446.e: Luxembourg only borders Belgium, France and Germany. The Netherlands lies further north.
50446.m: Luxembourg borders Belgium, France and Germany.

50447.q: What has been free in Luxembourg since 2020?
50447.e: Since 2020, you can travel by bus, tram and train all over Luxembourg without a ticket. Luxembourg was the first country in the world to do this.
50447.m: In Luxembourg, buses and trains are free.

50448.q: What colours is the flag of Luxembourg?
50448.e: The flag has three horizontal stripes in red, white and light blue. It looks very similar to the flag of the Netherlands, only the blue is lighter.
50448.m: The flag of Luxembourg is red, white and light blue.

50449.q: What are the casemates in the city of Luxembourg?
50449.e: The casemates are long passages that were dug into the rock long ago. Soldiers could shelter there.
50449.m: The casemates are passages in the rock of Luxembourg.

50450.q: What does the name “Côte d'Azur” mean in English?
50450.e: “Côte” means coast and “azur” is a bright sky blue. The name suits the blue sea and sky.
50450.m: Côte d'Azur means Blue Coast in English.

50451.q: Which sea is the Côte d'Azur on?
50451.e: The Côte d'Azur is in the south-east of France on the Mediterranean. The water there is warm in summer.
50451.m: The Côte d'Azur is on the Mediterranean.

50452.q: Which is the largest city on the Côte d'Azur?
50452.e: Nice has around 340,000 inhabitants and is the largest city on this coast. It also has a large airport.
50452.m: Nice is the largest city on the Côte d'Azur.

50453.q: In which town on the Côte d'Azur is a famous film festival held every year?
50453.e: Film stars from all over the world meet in Cannes every May. Locarno in Ticino also has a well-known film festival, but not by the sea.
50453.m: Cannes has a famous film festival.

50454.q: In which city is the famous seafront promenade “Promenade des Anglais”?
50454.e: The Promenade des Anglais is a long path right by the sea in Nice. The name means “Promenade of the English”.
50454.m: The Promenade des Anglais is in Nice.

50455.q: What is the weather usually like on the Côte d'Azur in summer?
50455.e: The Côte d'Azur has a great many sunny days a year. The summers are hot and dry, the winters mild.
50455.m: On the Côte d'Azur it is usually warm and sunny in summer.

50456.q: Which mountains reach close to the sea on the Côte d'Azur?
50456.e: The Maritime Alps are the southernmost part of the Alps. They reach almost to the coast, so there you can swim and ski on the same day.
50456.m: On the Côte d'Azur the Alps reach close to the sea.

50457.q: What are many beaches on the Côte d'Azur made of?
50457.e: Many beaches there are made of round, smooth pebbles instead of fine sand. So beach shoes are handy.
50457.m: Many beaches on the Côte d'Azur have pebbles.

50458.e: Monaco is a principality. Albert II has been the Prince of Monaco since 2005 (as of 2025).
50458.m: Monaco is ruled by a prince.

50459.q: What can you watch every day in front of the Prince's Palace in Monaco?
50459.e: Every day shortly before noon, the guards in front of the palace change in a small ceremony. Many tourists watch.
50459.m: There is a changing of the guard in front of the Prince's Palace every day.

50460.q: Which motor race goes through the streets of Monaco every year?
50460.e: At the Monaco Grand Prix, Formula 1 cars race through narrow streets and bends. The track even goes through a tunnel.
50460.m: Formula 1 races through the streets of Monaco.

50461.q: What is the name of a well-known district of Monaco with a famous casino?
50461.e: Monte Carlo is a district of Monaco. It has a magnificent casino and many luxury hotels.
50461.m: Monte Carlo is a district of Monaco.

50462.q: Which country does Monaco border on land?
50462.e: On the land side, Monaco is completely surrounded by France. On the other side is the sea.

50463.q: What colours is the flag of Monaco?
50463.e: The flag of Monaco is red at the top and white at the bottom. These are the colours of the princely family.
50463.m: The flag of Monaco is red and white.

50464.q: Which famous museum in Monaco shows fish and other sea creatures?
50464.e: The Oceanographic Museum stands on a cliff right above the sea. It has a large aquarium with many sea creatures.
50464.m: In Monaco, the Oceanographic Museum shows sea creatures.

50465.q: What money do you pay with in Monaco?
50465.e: Monaco is not part of the European Union but still uses the euro. It is even allowed to mint its own euro coins.
50465.m: In Monaco you pay with euros.

50466.q: How many horses pull the chariot on the Brandenburg Gate?
50466.e: The chariot on top of the gate is pulled by four horses. A chariot with four horses is called a quadriga.

50467.q: Who drives the chariot on the Brandenburg Gate?
50467.e: Victoria, the goddess of victory, stands on the chariot. She holds a staff with an eagle.
50467.m: Victoria, the goddess of victory, drives the quadriga.

50468.q: What is the Brandenburg Gate built from?
50468.e: The gate was built from light sandstone more than 200 years ago.
50468.m: The Brandenburg Gate is made of sandstone.

50469.q: What used to stand right next to the Brandenburg Gate and divided Berlin into two parts?
50469.e: For almost 30 years, the Berlin Wall stood right next to the gate. Since the fall of the Wall in 1989, people can walk through it again.
50469.m: The Berlin Wall used to stand by the Brandenburg Gate.

50470.q: Which celebration do many people mark every year with fireworks in front of the Brandenburg Gate?
50470.e: On the night before 1 January there is a big New Year's Eve party with fireworks in front of the gate.
50470.m: People celebrate New Year's Eve in front of the Brandenburg Gate.

50472.q: Which German city has the largest port in Germany?
50472.e: Hamburg has the largest port in Germany. Every day, big ships from all over the world arrive there.
50472.m: Germany's largest port is in Hamburg.

50473.q: Which river is the port of Hamburg on?
50473.e: The port of Hamburg is on the Elbe. The ships travel along the river to the sea.

50474.q: What are the big metal boxes that ships use to carry goods called?
50474.e: Containers are big boxes made of metal. They fit on ships, lorries and trains.
50474.m: Containers are big boxes for goods.

50475.q: What is used to lift the containers off the ships in the port of Hamburg?
50475.e: Huge cranes lift the heavy containers off the ship and put them down on land.
50475.m: Cranes lift containers off the ships.

50476.q: What is the old district of red-brick warehouses at the port of Hamburg called?
50476.e: Coffee, tea and spices used to be stored in the Speicherstadt. It has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2015.
50476.m: The Speicherstadt is an old warehouse district in Hamburg.

50477.q: Which famous concert hall with a wavy glass roof stands at the port of Hamburg?
50477.e: The Elbphilharmonie stands on top of an old warehouse. Its roof looks like waves.
50477.m: The Elbphilharmonie is a concert hall at the port of Hamburg.

50478.q: Which market takes place at the port in Hamburg early every Sunday morning?
50478.e: The Hamburg fish market starts very early on Sundays. It sells not only fish but also fruit and much more.
50478.m: Hamburg has its fish market on Sunday mornings.

50479.q: Which big festival does Hamburg celebrate at the port every year in May?
50479.e: Many ships and visitors come for the port's birthday. There are parades on the water and fireworks.
50479.m: Hamburg celebrates the port's birthday every year.

50480.q: Which sea do ships sail into when they leave the port of Hamburg?
50480.e: The river at Hamburg flows into the North Sea. From there, ships sail all over the world.
50480.m: Ships from the port of Hamburg sail into the North Sea.

50481.q: Which big folk festival takes place in Munich every year?
50481.e: Oktoberfest is one of the biggest folk festivals in the world. It actually starts in September.

50482.q: Munich is the capital of which German state?
50482.e: Munich is the capital of Bavaria. Bavaria is in the south of Germany.
50482.m: Munich is the capital of Bavaria.

50483.q: What is the most famous square in the centre of Munich called?
50483.e: Marienplatz is the centre of Munich. The New Town Hall stands there.
50483.m: Marienplatz is in the centre of Munich.

50484.q: What dances to music in the tower of Munich's town hall?
50484.e: There is a glockenspiel in the tower of the New Town Hall. Colourful figures turn and dance to it.
50484.m: Figures dance at the glockenspiel in Munich.

50485.q: How many towers does the Frauenkirche in Munich have?
50485.e: The Frauenkirche has two towers with round domes. They are a landmark of Munich.

50486.e: The Isar flows through Munich. In summer, lots of people lie in the sun on its banks.

50487.q: What is the huge park in Munich called?
50487.e: The English Garden is one of the largest city parks in the world. It is even bigger than Central Park in New York.
50487.m: The big park in Munich is called the English Garden.

50488.q: What can you see at Hellabrunn Zoo in Munich?
a: Animals from all over the world
50488.e: Hellabrunn Zoo is in the south of Munich on the Isar. Animals from all over the world live there.
50488.m: Animals from all over the world live at Hellabrunn Zoo in Munich.

50489.q: What is the big museum of technology and science in Munich called?
50489.e: The Deutsches Museum is one of the largest technology museums in the world. You can see aeroplanes, ships and mines there.
50489.m: The Deutsches Museum in Munich shows technology.

50490.q: Which king had Neuschwanstein Castle built?
50490.e: King Ludwig II of Bavaria had the castle built. He is also called the Fairy Tale King.
50490.m: King Ludwig II had Neuschwanstein built.

50491.q: In which country is Neuschwanstein Castle?
50491.e: Neuschwanstein is in the south of Germany, near the border with Austria.

50492.q: What is Neuschwanstein often called because of how it looks?
50492.e: With its many white towers, Neuschwanstein looks like a castle from a fairy tale.
50492.m: Neuschwanstein is called a fairy-tale castle.

50493.q: Neuschwanstein Castle stands at the edge of which mountain range?
50493.e: The castle stands on a rock in front of the mountains of the Alps.
50493.m: Neuschwanstein stands at the edge of the Alps.

50494.q: The wall paintings in Neuschwanstein show stories from the operas of which composer?
50494.e: The king was a great fan of Richard Wagner's operas. So many pictures in the castle show legends from these operas.
50494.m: Neuschwanstein Castle has paintings about Wagner's operas.

50495.q: Was Neuschwanstein Castle ever completely finished?
50495.e: When the king died in 1886, the castle was not yet finished. Many rooms stayed empty.

50497.q: How long did the king live in Neuschwanstein Castle?
50497.e: Altogether the king lived in the castle for only about 170 days. Shortly afterwards he died.
50497.m: The king only lived in Neuschwanstein for a short time.

50498.q: Which kind of clock is typical of the Black Forest?
50498.e: Cuckoo clocks have been made in the Black Forest for a long time. Every full hour, a little bird calls out.
50498.m: The cuckoo clock comes from the Black Forest.

50499.q: Apart from cherries, what goes into a Black Forest gateau?
50499.e: A Black Forest gateau has layers of chocolate sponge, cream and cherries.
50499.m: Black Forest gateau is made with cherries and cream.

50500.q: What is on the famous Bollenhut hat from the Black Forest?
50500.e: The Bollenhut has big pompoms made of wool. Red pompoms are worn by women who are not yet married.
